candidates <- c(
  dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)),

  file.path(Sys.getenv("QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR"), "blog", "posts", "post3"),
  file.path(getwd(), "blog", "posts", "post3")
)
valid <- vapply(candidates, function(p) {
  file.exists(file.path(p, "R", "01_prepare.R")) &&
    file.exists(file.path(p, "data", "raw", "README.md"))
}, logical(1))
if (!any(valid)) stop("Keep index.qmd, R and data together inside post3.")

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.2, out.width = "100%"
)
source("R/01_prepare.R")
source("R/02_analyze.R")
cps <- load_and_prepare_cps("data/raw")
analysis <- analyze_cps(cps, "results")
premium <- analysis$overall_premium
changes <- analysis$overall_change
sex_changes <- analysis$sex_change
gender <- analysis$gender_premium
first_year <- analysis$first_year
latest_year <- analysis$latest_year
dollar_year <- analysis$dollar_year
first <- premium[premium$income_year == first_year, ]
last <- premium[premium$income_year == latest_year, ]
ba_change <- changes$change_pct[changes$education == "Bachelor's"]
hs_change <- changes$change_pct[changes$education == "High school"]
change_for <- function(sex, degree) {
  sex_changes$change_pct[
    sex_changes$sex_group == sex & sex_changes$education == degree
  ]
}
women_ba <- change_for("Women", "Bachelor's")
women_hs <- change_for("Women", "High school")
men_ba <- change_for("Men", "Bachelor's")
men_hs <- change_for("Men", "High school")
latest_gender <- gender[gender$income_year == latest_year, ]
women_premium <- latest_gender$premium_pct[latest_gender$sex_group == "Women"]
men_premium <- latest_gender$premium_pct[latest_gender$sex_group == "Men"]
money <- function(x) scales::dollar(x, accuracy = 1)
pct <- function(x) paste0(sprintf("%.1f", x), "%")
# These checks protect the written interpretation if the extract changes.
if (latest_year != 2024 || first_year != 2000 ||
    last$premium_pct <= first$premium_pct || abs(ba_change) >= 1 ||
    hs_change >= 0 || women_ba <= 0 || women_hs >= 0 ||
    men_ba >= 0 || men_hs >= 0 ||
    abs(women_premium - men_premium) >= 1) {
  stop("The extract changes the findings. Review the article before publishing.")
}
```

A university degree can provide an earnings advantage even when graduates' pay barely increases. That distinction matters when interpreting claims about the financial value of college: earning more than another group is different from being able to buy more than earlier graduates. **Did a larger college earnings premium between `r first_year` and `r latest_year` mean that bachelor's graduates earned substantially more in real terms?**

In this CPS comparison, the answer is no. The relative gap widened modestly, while the pooled median for bachelor's graduates ended almost where it began. The three figures separate the relative comparison from purchasing power, then check whether the pooled result describes women and men equally well.

## The relative advantage became slightly larger

```{r premium-trend, fig.cap="Figure 1. Bachelor's premium relative to high-school graduates. Points are the selected income years; lines connect those observations.", fig.alt="A line shows the bachelor's earnings premium fluctuating between selected income years. Its endpoint rises from about 60 percent in 2000 to 64 percent in 2024, without a steady upward trend."}
analysis$premium_plot
```

I define the premium as the weighted median weekly earnings of bachelor's graduates divided by the corresponding high-school median, minus one. A 60% premium means the bachelor's median is 1.6 times the high-school median; it does not mean college raises every student's earnings by 60%.

Figure 1 puts the premium at **`r pct(first$premium_pct)` in `r first_year` and `r pct(last$premium_pct)` in `r latest_year`**, an increase of `r sprintf("%.1f", last$premium_pct - first$premium_pct)` percentage points. The intervening observations fluctuate, so the endpoints should not be described as a steady rise.

## A bigger ratio need not mean a bigger paycheck

```{r real-earnings, fig.cap="Figure 2. Weighted median weekly wage and salary income, expressed in 2024 dollars.", fig.alt="Two lines compare real weekly earnings for bachelor's and high-school graduates. The bachelor's median begins and ends near 1577 dollars; the high-school median falls from about 983 to 962 dollars."}
analysis$earnings_plot
```

The bachelor's median moved from **`r money(first[["Bachelor's"]])` to `r money(last[["Bachelor's"]])` per week**, a real change of only `r pct(ba_change)`. The high-school median fell from `r money(first[["High school"]])` to `r money(last[["High school"]])`, or `r pct(abs(hs_change))`.

These endpoints explain the apparent puzzle. A nearly unchanged numerator divided by a smaller denominator produces a larger relative premium. College graduates retained a sizable earnings advantage, but that advantage is not evidence of a large gain in their purchasing power over this period. This is an arithmetic description of group medians, not an explanation of what caused either group's earnings to change.

For a reader thinking about living standards, the dollar series is the relevant check: it puts both years on the same purchasing-power scale. The percentage premium instead answers how far apart two groups are. Neither measure alone tells us whether tuition was worthwhile, because these data do not include students' costs or their alternative career paths.

## The pooled result is not everyone's experience

```{r earnings-change-by-sex, fig.cap="Figure 3. Percentage change in each group's weighted median real weekly earnings from 2000 to 2024. These are repeated cross-sections, not individual earnings histories.", fig.alt="Four bars show changes between 2000 and 2024. Bachelor's earnings rise modestly among women and decline among men. High-school earnings decline within both sex categories."}
analysis$sex_change_plot
```

For women, the bachelor's median increased `r pct(women_ba)`, while the high-school median declined `r pct(abs(women_hs))`. For men, both fell: `r pct(abs(men_ba))` for bachelor's graduates and `r pct(abs(men_hs))` for high-school graduates. A relative advantage can therefore widen even when both comparison groups lose purchasing power.

By `r latest_year`, the within-sex premiums were `r pct(women_premium)` for women and `r pct(men_premium)` for men: very close. Without uncertainty estimates, that small difference should not be presented as a clear gender difference. The figures also do not follow the same workers over time or establish individual career paths.

## What the figures can tell us

The sample uses [IPUMS CPS ASEC](https://cps.ipums.org/cps/) wage and salary workers ages 25–64 who worked 50–52 weeks and usually at least 35 hours weekly. Income refers to the preceding calendar year; annual wage income is divided by weeks worked. Every median uses the person weight [ASECWT](https://cps.ipums.org/cps/sample_weights.shtml). Published [CPI99 factors](https://cps.ipums.org/cps/cpi99.shtml), stored in the code, express earnings in `r dollar_year` dollars; the extract does not need a CPI99 variable.

These restrictions exclude people with absent or unstable employment. Changing group composition, top coding, nonresponse and sampling error can affect medians. The comparison does not control for occupation, experience, college costs or selection into education, and cannot measure college's causal return.

**The takeaway: check both the earnings gap and the earnings levels.** A larger relative college advantage can coexist with little improvement in graduates' real median pay. It answers a different question from whether college paid off for a particular student.

[Code, data definitions and replication instructions](https://github.com/augenstern118/testrepo/tree/main/blog/posts/post3) accompany the article; raw IPUMS microdata require separate access.
